I use this example to show that Mattern is not just taking us through Galen's early life and training but interpreting intellectual affiliations that are often clouded in polemic and apparent inconsistency in Galen's account, depending on rhetorical need and the kind of medical work that he was writing at that moment.

## Extract

How, if you are not the lifetime Galen scholar Vivian Nutton (who, happily, endorses this book on the back cover), do you write a biography of a writer who is self-aggrandizing, self-confident, full of anecdotes of his own distinction, and who was to become the most influential medical writer in Western culture (from perhaps 162 to 1850 a.d.)? How do you write a biography of any ancient person for that matter? --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Notes

^{1}

It should be noted that the events of Galen’s life are mainly attested only by Galen’s own writings, with little or no independent confirmation, and also that it is often impossible to assign clear dates to his works, which were revised at different times throughout his life. The dates given represent best guesses, and in many cases correspond to the date of final writing-up of a work previously given in oral or draft form.

^{2}

On Galen’s name, and in particular whether he also bore a family name or nomen gentilicium (either the traditionally ascribed Claudius or Aelius), which would imply his possession of Roman citizenship, see

V. Nutton, “What’s in a Nomen: Vlatadon 14 and an Old Theory Resurrected,” in B. Holmes and K.-D. Fischer (eds.), The Frontiers of Ancient Science: Essays in Honor of Heinrich von Staden, De Gruyter, 451–62
